title: Paid by the City, with no return on file or a very late one
question: Which organizations were paid by the City in a year for which no federal tax return can be found, and which filed more than a year after the last permitted date?
finding: Of 485 organizations checked, 21 were paid $100,000 or more by the City in at least one fiscal year for which no return is on file, $106.8 million in those years; for 11 of them ($5.9 million) the records give no reason such as church status or a first return in a later year, the largest being The Gubbio Project ($1.4 million, fiscal 2025). 12 returns were filed more than a year after the last date allowed with an extension, the latest 577 days after it (Bindlestiff Studio, year ended 31 December 2023); 34 were more than 180 days after it.
how: Returns on file are every tax period listed for the organization's employer number in the IRS e-file index for 2020 to 2026 or in ProPublica's mirror of IRS filings, which includes paper returns. A City fiscal year counts as covered when a tax year ending in that calendar year is on file (a year ending in early January counts as the December before); fiscal years are tested from 2020 up to the organization's latest year whose extended due date had passed when the files were pulled. Listed when City payments in an uncovered fiscal year were $100,000 or more. Lateness is the filing timestamp of the first version of each return against the extended due date, the 15th day of the eleventh month after the year-end; returns more than 365 days past that date are listed.
limits: No return on file is not the same as no return filed. Churches and arms of government need not file, a subsidiary can be covered by a parent's group return, a paper return may not have reached the public files, and the newest returns take months to be released; the last column gives what the IRS master file and the filing history say. A payee matched to the wrong tax number will look as if it never files. A late return is still a return, and deadlines are sometimes postponed for a whole area, for example after a disaster; these files do not record such postponements. 15 payee names could not be tied to any tax number and are not tested at all. City money is taken from the Controller's table of every payment, not from its narrower nonprofit-spending table, which keeps contracted services only. Left out of it, each picked out by the payment file's own label, are: loans; money the City collects for a benefit district and hands over (the district's own assessments); benefit-plan payments from a trust fund; and debt service. For 23 of the 485 organizations matched here that makes the City figure at least $1 million and 10% higher over fiscal 2019 to 2026, $1.36 billion higher in all. The figure keeps grants and contracts the nonprofit-spending table lacks, emergency purchases, and aid paid through an organization (day care assistance, rent assistance paid on behalf of clients, in-home care contract payments). Part of that aid passes on to others, so it is a real City payment but not all of it is payment for the organization's own work. A return may not count money that passes through as revenue. For the organizations matched here, that leaves out $78.8 million of loans (9 organizations), $425.1 million of money the City collected for a benefit district and handed over (14 organizations) and $495.1 million of benefit-plan payments from a trust fund (1 organization), fiscal 2019 to 2026. District assessments are covered on the screen “Benefit districts: assessments in, City grants on top”, which keeps assessments and City grants apart. The fiscal year is the one printed on each payment, which can be later than the year the payment was made. A pattern here is a reason to ask for the audited statements, not a finding.
